exercises.title: Linear interpolation
exercises.description: Find the linear interpolant through $(1, 2)$ and $(3, 8)$ and evaluate it at $x = 2$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Two points ⇒ line (degree $\le 1$).

Step 3: Evaluating
$p(2) = 2 + 3 = 5$ (exactly the average $\frac{2+8}{2}$).

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Linear interpolation is the simplest case; at the midpoint it gives the average.

exercises.title: Lagrange basis polynomial
exercises.description: For the nodes $0, 1, 3$ state the basis polynomial $L_1$ and check $L_1(0) = 0$, $L_1(1) = 1$, $L_1(3) = 0$. Compute $L_1(2)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$L_1(x) = \dfrac{(x - x_0)(x - x_2)}{(x_1 - x_0)(x_1 - x_2)}$.

Step 2: Setting up
$L_1(x) = \dfrac{(x - 0)(x - 3)}{(1 - 0)(1 - 3)} = \dfrac{x(x-3)}{-2} = -\tfrac12 x(x - 3)$.

Step 4: Value
$L_1(2) = -\tfrac12\cdot 2\cdot(-1) = 1$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The numerator omits the own node $x_i$; the denominator is the same product evaluated at $x_i$.

exercises.title: Interpolation polynomial via Lagrange
exercises.description: Use the Lagrange form to find the polynomial through $(-1, 1)$, $(0, 0)$, $(1, 1)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$p = \sum y_iL_i$; because $y_1 = 0$ one term drops out.

Step 2: Basis polynomials
$L_{-1} = \tfrac12 x(x - 1)$, $L_0 = 1 - x^2$, $L_1 = \tfrac12 x(x + 1)$.

Step 3: Assembling
$p = 1\cdot\tfrac12 x(x-1) + 0\cdot L_0 + 1\cdot\tfrac12 x(x+1) = \tfrac12(x^2 - x + x^2 + x) = x^2$.

Step 4: Check
$p(-1) = 1$, $p(0) = 0$, $p(1) = 1$ ✓. The polynomial is $p(x) = x^2$ (degree $2$).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Points that already lie on a simple curve return exactly that curve.

exercises.title: First-order divided differences
exercises.description: Compute the divided-difference scheme for $(1,1), (2,4), (4,16)$ and state the Newton polynomial.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
First the differences of first, then second order.

Step 4: Polynomial
$p(x) = 1 + 3(x - 1) + 1\cdot(x - 1)(x - 2)$. Check: $p(4) = 1 + 9 + 6 = 16$ ✓. Expanded $p(x) = x^2$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The denominator is the difference of the outer nodes, not of the neighbours.

exercises.title: Evaluating the Newton form
exercises.description: Evaluate $p(x) = 2 + 3(x-1) + 0.5(x-1)(x-3)$ at $x = 2$ using the Horner scheme.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Nest from the inside out: $2 + (x-1)\bigl(3 + 0.5(x-3)\bigr)$.

Step 3: Check
Directly: $2 + 3 + 0.5\cdot 1\cdot(-1) = 4.5$ ✓.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Horner needs $n$ multiplications – fewer than multiplying out the products.

exercises.title: Determining the degree
exercises.description: Five points $(0,1), (1,2), (2,5), (3,10), (4,17)$: what is the degree of the interpolation polynomial? (Hint: divided differences, i.e. difference scheme.)
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
The degree is the order from which all divided differences are $0$.

Step 2: Differences
First order: $1, 3, 5, 7$. Second order (step $1$, divide by $2$): $1, 1, 1$. Third order: $0, 0$.

Step 3: Result
Degree $2$: $p(x) = 1 + x + x(x-1) = x^2 + 1$. Five points but only degree $2$ – the bound “$\le n = 4$” is not attained.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
Degree $\le n$, not $= n$: vanishing divided differences lower the degree.

exercises.title: Solving the Vandermonde system
exercises.description: Set up and solve the Vandermonde system for the points $(1,2), (2,3), (3,6)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Ansatz $p = a_0 + a_1x + a_2x^2$.

Step 2: System
$\begin{pmatrix}1&1&1\\1&2&4\\1&3&9\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a_0\\a_1\\a_2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}2\\3\\6\end{pmatrix}$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The system is practical only for small $n$ – because of its conditioning (cf. 4.2).

exercises.title: Justifying uniqueness
exercises.description: Explain why there is at most one polynomial of degree $\le n$ through $n+1$ points with distinct nodes.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Suppose there are two: $p$ and $q$.

Step 2: Difference
$r = p - q$ has degree $\le n$ and $r(x_i) = p(x_i) - q(x_i) = y_i - y_i = 0$ for $i = 0, \dots, n$.

Step 3: Contradiction
A nonzero polynomial of degree $\le n$ has at most $n$ roots, but $r$ has $n+1$. So $r \equiv 0$ and $p = q$.

Step 4: Takeaway: What matters
The representation (Lagrange, Newton, monomials) differs – the polynomial itself is always the same.

exercises.title: Divided-difference scheme (4 points)
exercises.description: Find the Newton polynomial through $(0,1), (1,3), (2,2), (3,5)$ and check it at $x = 3$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Build the scheme up to third order.

Step 4: Third order
$f[0,1,2,3] = (2 + 1.5)/3 = \tfrac76$.

Step 5: Polynomial and check
$p(x) = 1 + 2x - 1.5x(x-1) + \tfrac76 x(x-1)(x-2)$. $p(3) = 1 + 6 - 9 + 7 = 5$ ✓.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
The coefficients sit on the top diagonal of the scheme.

exercises.title: Adding a point
exercises.description: The polynomial through $(0,0), (1,1), (2,8)$ is known. Add $(3,27)$ without starting over.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Newton form: only one new term with the new divided difference.

Step 4: New polynomial
$p_3(x) = x + 3x(x-1) + x(x-1)(x-2)$. Expanded $x + 3x^2 - 3x + x^3 - 3x^2 + 2x = x^3$ ✓ (the data come from $x^3$).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The cost for the new point is $O(n)$ – with Lagrange all $L_i$ would have to be rebuilt.

exercises.title: Neville scheme at one point
exercises.description: Use the Neville–Aitken scheme to compute the value of the interpolation polynomial through $(0,1), (1,3), (2,2)$ at $x = 1.5$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$P_{i,i+1} = \dfrac{(x - x_i)P_{i+1} - (x - x_{i+1})P_i}{x_{i+1} - x_i}$ and analogously for higher levels.

Step 4: Check
Newton form: $1 + 2\cdot1.5 - 1.5\cdot 1.5\cdot 0.5 = 1 + 3 - 1.125 = 2.875$ ✓.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Neville yields only the value, not the polynomial – ideal for single evaluations or extrapolations (Romberg!).

exercises.title: Error estimate for sin
exercises.description: Let $p$ be the interpolation polynomial of $\sin x$ at the nodes $0, 0.5, 1$. Estimate the error at $x = 0.25$ and compare with the true error ($p(0.25) = 0.25439$, $\sin 0.25 = 0.24740$).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Error formula with $n = 2$: $\dfrac{|f'''(\xi)|}{3!}\,|x(x - 0.5)(x - 1)|$.

Step 2: Derivative
$f''' = -\cos x$, so $|f'''| \le 1$.

Step 3: Node polynomial
$|0.25\cdot(-0.25)\cdot(-0.75)| = 0.046875$.

Step 4: Bound
$|\text{error}| \le \dfrac{1}{6}\cdot 0.046875 = 0.0078$.

Step 5: Comparison
True error $|0.25439 - 0.24740| = 0.0070 \le 0.0078$ ✓ – the bound is almost tight.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
The error formula holds with an unknown $\xi$ – one bounds $f^{(n+1)}$ by its maximum.

exercises.title: Chebyshev nodes for n = 2
exercises.description: Compute the Chebyshev nodes for $n = 2$ on $[-1,1]$ and on $[0,4]$ and compare $\max|\prod(x - x_i)|$ with that of the equidistant nodes $-1, 0, 1$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$x_k = \cos\dfrac{(2k+1)\pi}{2n+2}$, $k = 0, 1, 2$.

Step 4: Comparison
Chebyshev: $\max|x(x^2 - 0.75)| = 2^{-2} = 0.25$. Equidistant: $\max|x(x^2-1)| = \frac{2}{3\sqrt3} = 0.385$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Already at $n = 2$ it is $35\%$ less; for high $n$ this decides between convergence and divergence.

exercises.title: Lagrange vs. Newton: cost
exercises.description: For $n+1$ nodes compare the cost of (a) setting up, (b) evaluating at one point, (c) adding a node for the Lagrange form and the Newton form.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Count operations in $O$ notation.

Step 2: Newton
(a) scheme: $O(n^2)$. (b) Horner: $O(n)$. (c) new diagonal: $O(n)$.

Step 3: Lagrange
(a) no setup. (b) Each $L_i$ costs $O(n)$, in total $O(n^2)$ (with the barycentric form $O(n)$ after $O(n^2)$ preprocessing). (c) new: everything $O(n^2)$.

Step 4: Recommendation
Many evaluations, fixed data: Newton or barycentric Lagrange form. Growing data: Newton. Theory and derivations: Lagrange.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
All three representations give the same polynomial; they differ only in cost and conditioning.

exercises.title: Hermite interpolation
exercises.description: Find the polynomial of degree $\le 2$ with $p(0) = 1$, $p'(0) = 1$, $p(1) = 3$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Nodes $0, 0, 1$ in the Newton form; $f[0,0] = p'(0)$.

Step 3: Polynomial
$p(x) = 1 + 1\cdot(x - 0) + 1\cdot(x - 0)(x - 0) = 1 + x + x^2$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Three conditions ⇒ degree $\le 2$. Derivative conditions count like point conditions.

exercises.title: Estimating √2 by interpolation
exercises.description: Interpolate $f(x) = \sqrt x$ at the nodes $1, 4, 9$ (values $1, 2, 3$) and estimate $\sqrt 2$ by $p(2)$. How large is the error?
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Divided differences with the nodes $1, 4, 9$.

Step 2: Scheme
$f[1,4] = \tfrac13$, $f[4,9] = \tfrac15$, $f[1,4,9] = \dfrac{\tfrac15 - \tfrac13}{9 - 1} = -\tfrac{1}{60}$.

Step 4: Error
$\sqrt2 = 1.4142$, error $0.0475$ ($\approx 3.4\%$). The error formula explains this: $f''' = \tfrac38x^{-5/2}$ is large for $x$ near $1$, and the nodes are far apart.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Interpolation works well for smooth functions and closely spaced nodes – poorly when the derivatives nearby are large.

exercises.title: Proving the error formula
exercises.description: Prove: for $f \in C^{n+1}$ and $x \notin \{x_i\}$ we have $f(x) - p(x) = \dfrac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}\omega(x)$ with $\omega(t) = \prod(t - x_i)$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Construct an auxiliary function with $n+2$ roots and apply Rolle's theorem $n+1$ times.

Step 2: Auxiliary function
$g(t) = f(t) - p(t) - c\,\omega(t)$ with $c = \dfrac{f(x) - p(x)}{\omega(x)}$. Then $g(x_i) = 0$ ($i = 0..n$) and $g(x) = 0$: $n+2$ roots.

Step 3: Rolle
$g'$ has $n+1$ roots, $g''$ has $n$, …, $g^{(n+1)}$ has at least one: $g^{(n+1)}(\xi) = 0$.

Step 4: Evaluating the derivative
$p^{(n+1)} = 0$ (degree $\le n$), $\omega^{(n+1)} = (n+1)!$. So $0 = f^{(n+1)}(\xi) - c\,(n+1)!$.

Step 5: Result
$c = \dfrac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}$, i.e. $f(x) - p(x) = \dfrac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}\omega(x)$.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
The pattern – auxiliary function plus Rolle – returns for quadrature errors (4.11).

exercises.title: Recursion for divided differences
exercises.description: Show: the leading coefficient (of $x^n$) of the interpolation polynomial through $x_0,\dots,x_n$ is $f[x_0,\dots,x_n]$, and $f[x_0,\dots,x_n] = \dfrac{f[x_1,\dots,x_n] - f[x_0,\dots,x_{n-1}]}{x_n - x_0}$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Construct $p$ from the two interpolation polynomials with one node fewer each.

Step 2: Newton form
In $p = \sum_k a_k\prod_{j<k}(x - x_j)$ the last term has leading coefficient $a_n$; the others have degree $< n$. So $a_n = f[x_0..x_n]$ is the coefficient of $x^n$.

Step 3: Two partial polynomials
$p_a$ interpolates at $x_0..x_{n-1}$, $p_b$ at $x_1..x_n$ (both degree $\le n-1$). Then $p(x) = \dfrac{(x - x_0)\,p_b(x) - (x - x_n)\,p_a(x)}{x_n - x_0}$ (Aitken–Neville).

Step 4: Checking
At $x_0$: $p = \dfrac{-(x_0 - x_n)p_a(x_0)}{x_n - x_0} = p_a(x_0) = y_0$ ✓; at $x_n$ analogously; at an inner $x_i$: $p_a = p_b = y_i$ ✓.

Step 5: Coefficient of xⁿ
The leading coefficient of $(x - x_0)p_b - (x - x_n)p_a$ is $\mathrm{lc}(p_b) - \mathrm{lc}(p_a) = f[x_1..x_n] - f[x_0..x_{n-1}]$ (induction). Dividing by $x_n - x_0$ gives the recursion.

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
This proves the divided-difference scheme – and Neville along with it.

exercises.title: Σ L_i(x) = 1 and relatives
exercises.description: Prove $\sum_i L_i(x) = 1$ and $\sum_i x_iL_i(x) = x$ for all $x$ (nodes $x_0,\dots,x_n$, $n \ge 1$).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Interpolate the functions $1$ and $x$ – both are polynomials of degree $\le n$.

Step 2: Constant
The data $y_i = 1$ are interpolated by the polynomial $q \equiv 1$ (degree $0 \le n$). By uniqueness $q = \sum y_iL_i = \sum L_i$, so $\sum L_i(x) = 1$.

Step 3: Identity
The data $y_i = x_i$ are interpolated by $r(x) = x$ (degree $1 \le n$). So $\sum x_iL_i(x) = x$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The weights $L_i(x)$ form an “affine combination” of the function values: sum $1$, but individual $L_i$ can be negative.

exercises.title: Lebesgue constant qualitatively
exercises.description: The Lebesgue constant $\Lambda_n = \max_x \sum_i|L_i(x)|$ measures the conditioning of interpolation. Compute $\Lambda_2$ for the nodes $-1, 0, 1$ and justify $\|p\|_\infty \le \Lambda_n\max|y_i|$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Triangle inequality on $p = \sum y_iL_i$.

Step 2: Estimate
$|p(x)| \le \sum|y_i||L_i(x)| \le \max|y_i|\sum|L_i(x)| \le \Lambda_n\max|y_i|$. So data are amplified by at most $\Lambda_n$.

Step 4: Growth
For equidistant nodes $\Lambda_n \sim 2^n/(e\,n\ln n)$ grows exponentially (e.g. $\Lambda_{10} \approx 30$), for Chebyshev nodes only logarithmically ($\Lambda_n \approx \tfrac2\pi\ln n$).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
$\Lambda_n$ is the condition number of interpolation – it explains the Runge phenomenon from the conditioning side.

exercises.title: Optimality of Chebyshev nodes
exercises.description: Explain why the roots of $T_{n+1}(x) = \cos\bigl((n+1)\arccos x\bigr)$ minimise $\max|\prod(x - x_i)|$.
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Properties of $T_{n+1}$: degree $n+1$, magnitude $\le 1$, $n+2$ extrema $\pm 1$ alternating.

Step 2: Normalisation
$T_{n+1}$ has leading coefficient $2^n$. So $\omega(x) = \prod(x - x_k) = 2^{-n}T_{n+1}(x)$ with $\max|\omega| = 2^{-n}$.

Step 3: Proof by contradiction
Suppose another monic polynomial $q$ of degree $n+1$ had $\max|q| < 2^{-n}$. Then $\omega - q$ has degree $\le n$ and changes sign at the $n+2$ extremal points of $T_{n+1}$.

Step 4: Contradiction
That gives $n+1$ roots for a polynomial of degree $\le n$ – hence $\omega - q \equiv 0$, contradicting $\max|q| < 2^{-n}$.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Equioscillation is the hallmark of minimax solutions.

exercises.title: Divided difference and derivative
exercises.description: Show $f[x_0,\dots,x_n] = \dfrac{f^{(n)}(\xi)}{n!}$ for some $\xi$ in the node interval and check it for $f = x^3$ (third divided difference) and $f = e^x$ (second, nodes $0, 1, 2$).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Compare the error formula with the Newton form using an additional point $x$.

Step 2: Idea
Newton: $f(x) - p_{n-1}(x) = f[x_0,\dots,x_{n-1},x]\prod_{i<n}(x - x_i)$. Error formula: $= \dfrac{f^{(n)}(\xi)}{n!}\prod_{i<n}(x - x_i)$.

Step 3: Consequence
Comparison: $f[x_0,\dots,x_{n-1},x] = \dfrac{f^{(n)}(\xi)}{n!}$. With $x = x_n$ the claim follows.

Step 4: Check x³
$f''' = 6$, so $f[x_0..x_3] = 6/3! = 1$ for arbitrary nodes – matches the scheme above (points of $x^3$ gave $1$).

Step 6: Takeaway: What matters
Divided differences are discrete derivatives: in the limit of coinciding nodes $f[x_0,\dots,x_0] = f^{(n)}(x_0)/n!$ (Hermite).

exercises.title: Error bound: Chebyshev vs. equidistant
exercises.description: For $f = e^x$ on $[-1,1]$ and $n = 3$ estimate the interpolation error (a) for equidistant nodes $-1, -\frac13, \frac13, 1$, (b) for Chebyshev nodes. Compare with the true errors ($0.00998$ and $0.00666$).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
$|f - p| \le \dfrac{\max|f^{(4)}|}{4!}\max|\omega|$ with $\max|f^{(4)}| = e$.

Step 2: (a) Equidistant
$\omega(x) = (x^2 - 1)(x^2 - \tfrac19)$; $\max|\omega| \approx 0.1975$ (inside the interval). Bound: $\dfrac{e}{24}\cdot 0.1975 = 0.0224$.

Step 3: (b) Chebyshev
$\max|\omega| = 2^{-3} = 0.125$. Bound: $\dfrac{e}{24}\cdot 0.125 = 0.0142$.

Step 4: Comparison
True errors: $0.00998$ (equidistant), $0.00666$ (Chebyshev) – both bounds hold, the ratio of the bounds $0.0224/0.0142 = 1.58$ matches the ratio of the true errors ($1.5$).

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
The bound reproduces the ratio of the errors well: the node polynomial is the deciding factor.

exercises.title: Extrapolation vs. interpolation
exercises.description: Interpolate $e^x$ at the nodes $0, 1, 2$ and compare the error at $x = 0.5$ (inside) and $x = 4$ (outside).
solutionSteps:
Step 1: Overview: What is asked?
Error formula: $\dfrac{e^\xi}{6}\,|x(x-1)(x-2)|$.

Step 2: Node polynomial
Inside: $|0.5\cdot(-0.5)\cdot(-1.5)| = 0.375$ (maximum on the interval $0.385$). Outside: $|4\cdot 3\cdot 2| = 24$.

Step 4: Consequence
Outside the node interval $|\omega|$ grows by a factor of $60$ compared to inside; the error grows by more than $180$. Extrapolation is risky.

Step 5: Takeaway: What matters
Polynomials leave the data interval with $x^n$ growth. High-degree polynomials are hardly suitable for extrapolation.
